best_for: Programmers and writers willing to spend a few evenings learning an editor they can reshape in Lisp and keep for decades, with notes, mail and agenda in the same window.

points.title: An editor you program
points.text: Almost every part of Emacs can be changed in Emacs Lisp, and a built-in package system installs extensions. The payoff is an editor that fits your habits instead of the reverse.

points.title: More than text in the box
points.text: Org mode for notes and planning, Gnus for mail and news, ERC for IRC, a calendar and a debugger front end all ship with it. Many users live in one Emacs window all day.

points.title: Expect a learning curve
points.text: The key bindings predate Windows and Mac conventions, and the built-in tutorial is the place to start. Emacs 31.1, out in August 2026, added a theme aimed at newcomers and turns on mouse support in terminals by default.

points.title: Free software under the GPL
points.text: Emacs is free of charge and licensed under the GPL, with no account, ads or paid tier. The GNU project treats Windows and macOS as secondary platforms that volunteers support.

points.title: Installer or zip on Windows
points.text: GNU publishes an installer .exe that adds shortcuts and a zip you unpack and start with `bin\runemacs.exe`. The 64-bit installer here installs for all users. MSYS2 users can install it with pacman instead.

points.title: No Mac download here
points.text: This page lists Windows and Linux only. On a Mac, GNU points to `brew install --cask emacs`, MacPorts' `emacs-app`, or the universal builds from the Emacs for OS X site.

points.title: Linux: distro packages come first
points.text: GNU recommends your distribution's package unless you always want the newest release. The Flatpak for x64 and Arm64 is a community package that Flathub says is not verified by or affiliated with the FSF. Windows keeps 11 versions here; Linux lists only the current one.
